title: What Does All Our Work Gain?
overview: A speaker writing as a king in Jerusalem looks at work, nature, history and his own search for wisdom, and finds that none of it brings real gain or full satisfaction.

parts.label: Who is speaking (v. 1)
parts.note: He calls himself Qoheleth, a Hebrew title for someone who gathers or addresses an assembly, so translations say 'Teacher' or 'Preacher'. Jewish and Christian tradition long identified him as Solomon, David's son, but many modern scholars think the book's late style of Hebrew points to a later writer speaking in Solomon's voice.

parts.label: The main claim (vv. 2-3)
parts.note: The key word, hevel, literally means breath or vapor; translations render it 'meaningless' or 'vanity', and scholars debate whether it means pointless, fleeting or beyond our grasp. Saying it twice means 'utterly', and verse 3 asks what people really gain from work 'under the sun', meaning life in this world.

parts.label: Nature going in circles (vv. 4-8)
parts.note: Generations pass while the earth stays, and the sun, wind and rivers keep moving yet always end up where they began. The picture seems meant to describe human life too: constant effort, with eyes and ears that are never satisfied.

parts.label: Nothing new, nothing remembered (vv. 9-11)
parts.note: What looks new has happened before, and people forget those who came before them and will be forgotten in turn. Many readers take this to mean that nothing new can truly satisfy us, not that new inventions never appear.

parts.label: The king's search (vv. 12-15)
parts.note: Writing as a king, he set out to understand everything people do, calling it a heavy task God has given humans and all of it a 'chasing' or 'striving' after wind, as translations put it. Verse 15 adds that what is bent cannot be straightened and what is missing cannot be counted, so wisdom cannot fix everything wrong with the world.

parts.label: Wisdom brings grief (vv. 16-18)
parts.note: He claims more wisdom than anyone before him in Jerusalem (translations differ on whether this means earlier rulers), and he studied foolishness too, but found this was also chasing wind. His conclusion is that the more you understand, the more clearly you see what is wrong, and the more it hurts.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the speaker's bleak verdict is the book's settled teaching, meant to show that life without God is empty, or an honest voice of doubt that the book records and then frames with its closing words in chapter 12.
think: What, if anything, makes effort feel worthwhile to you even when you know its results will not last?
